qt: to the Commission Mélanie Disdier (PfE), Catherine Griset (PfE), Valérie Deloge (PfE), Gilles Pennelle (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE), André Rougé (PfE) Subject:

Under Articles 4 and 12 of the Nature Restoration Regulation, Member States are required to restore terrestrial and forest ecosystems. At the same time, recent developments in the common organisation of the market in wine make it possible for support to be provided for the permanent grubbing-up of vineyards under national programmes. In Mediterranean regions, vineyards, agricultural land and pastoral areas act as natural firebreaks, limiting the spread of fires. However, their removing or abandoning them may encourage the continuous growth of combustible vegetation. With megafires on the rise in Southern Europe, the coherence of EU policies must be ensured. 1.

Has the Commission assessed the cumulative effects of the Regulation, the wine sector restructuring measures – including permanent grubbing-up – and the decline in pastoral activities on the risk of wildfires in the Mediterranean regions?
If not, how can it ensure that the combination of these policies will not lead to an increase in combustible biomass, the disappearance of mosaic landscapes and an increased risk of megafires?

Does it intend to systematically incorporate objectives relating to fire prevention, the maintenance of agricultural and pastoral activities, and the preservation of mosaic landscapes into the implementation of these policies?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.10.2026) The Commission recognises the decline in pastoral activities as one of the factors leading to increased wildfire risk in the Mediterranean region. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP)1 is the EU key funding instrument to provide support for agricultural activities that reduce wildfire risk in rural landscapes, such as pastoralism and extensive grazing. The implementation of the permanent grubbing-up of vineyards2 implies the complete elimination of vine stocks on the grubbed-up area, avoiding the accumulation of combustible biomass. To remain eligible for CAP support, farmers must pursue an agricultural activity on this area, implying either production (e.g. diversification) or maintenance of the area in a state which makes it suitable for grazing or cultivation. The Nature Restoration Regulation (NRR)3 contributes to building fire-resilient landscapes: restored forests are less vulnerable to fires thanks to a more diverse species composition, and restored wetlands and rewetted soils retain water in the landscape, which can slow down the spread of fire. The objectives of the NRR are therefore fully compatible with wildfire prevention goals. Member States must ensure that restoration measures in forest ecosystems duly consider forest fire risk4, and that their national restoration plans consider climate change impacts and natural disaster prevention goals5. The implementation of CAP and NRR relies on objectives and priorities defined in national plans based on the local context and needs, including wildfire risk.
